The region enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}-1$ and $y=-\frac{3}{2}x$ for $x\in [-2,\frac{1}{2}]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=5.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7aad98fe0513514aa8827bea4e9ffbac5b70bcb8da7923effd789988c81e286f.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=-\frac{3}{2}x,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{2}-1.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{2}-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/623b59b7aca8b33c6149ac6b0916d1eeb425adc3f74568868383806cd9b03b12.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}[\,(5)-({x}^{2}-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[6-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=-\frac{3}{2}x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c0467a3bf02287589f897586a1358e4abb02759134b6b58622125319dc7331da.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[\,(5)-(-\frac{3}{2}x)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[5+\frac{3}{2}x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[6-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[5+\frac{3}{2}x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}({[6-{x}^{2}]}^{2}-{[5+\frac{3}{2}x]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =x \\ {x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/82783afd970ec3f0e90a8b97a12207b0ed8cbf82323e0512e9fe36b99a6fdc2f.png)

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=x,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-({x}^{3})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}-{[2-x]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+{y}^{2} & =16\,⟹\,x=16-{y}^{2} \\ x+4y & =16\,⟹\,x=16-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/f39f9f399ea4d0e65a499f34d41158ddbaf5319a02e057e097b4f80c8197ba9e.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=16-{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=16-4y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=16-4y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/47d985510b37b7a14e82dfc20bc136694e7ba2e17172b35be45ebde88d238677.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[\,(16)-(16-4y)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[4y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=16-{y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/3e5494005010f3cfb8fb8b116c4b8ca91e8d3bf2712ad45c60f0766a2021b19a.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(16)-(16-{y}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[{y}^{2}]^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}({(4y)}^{2}-{({y}^{2})}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(16{y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(\frac{16{y}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{16(4)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(4)^{5}}{5})-0] \\  & =\pi (\frac{1024}{3}-\frac{1024}{5}) \\  & =\frac{2048\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

The region below enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt x$ and $y=x$ is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the line $y=1.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/362a92640ed68dfd5fa85f0338d95233003e9f8a1b059a5dffa2cda243a1411b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\eqalign{
 		x & =\sqrt x  \[3pt]
 		x-\sqrt x & = 0 \[3pt]
 		\sqrt x \left(\sqrt x - 1\right) &= 0 \[3pt]
 			x& = 0, 1
	}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/5456bed18c03e823c8e9388571b5671f5f476f5caa1085793314b57080b2b07c.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ and

- *leaves* though the outer curver $y=x.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/5136903876ed5ea811ebf28e0da905b5029b2c9311527fce9d0fed8e7bd1dd46.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(1)-(x)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c850643bb1c315d0516eff55d6270078504c1c98687cfac40e0c9b4b2c771b7c.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(1)-(\sqrt{x})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\eqalign{
V &= {\color{blue}V_{\text{outer}}} - {\color{brown}V_{\text{inner}}} \[5pt]
 		& = \pi \int_0^1 [1-x]^2 - \pi \int_0^1 [1-\sqrt x]^2\,\textrm d x \[5pt]
 		& = \pi \int_0^1 \left((1-x)^2 - (1-\sqrt x)^2\right) \,\textrm d x \[5pt]
 		& = \pi \int_0^1 (x^2-3x+2\sqrt x) \,\,\textrm d x \[5pt]
 		& = \pi\left. \left( \dfrac {1} 3 x^3 - \dfrac{3}{2} x^2 + \dfrac{4}{3} x^{3/2 } \ \right)\right|_0^1\[5pt] 
 		& =  \pi \left[\left( \dfrac {1}3 (1)^3 - \dfrac{3}{2}(1)^2  + \dfrac{4 }{3}(1)^{3/2 } \right) - (0) \right]\[5pt]
 		& =  \pi \left(\dfrac{1}3 - \dfrac{3}{2} +\dfrac{4}{3} \right)\[5pt]
 		& = \dfrac {\pi}{6} .
 		}
$$

\begin{aligned}{x}^{4} & =x \\ {x}^{4}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/49da0885bbf23e586b488e2b2a9bcaa0d923d3591833c9b8beb31a611c1d8b43.png)

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=x^4,$ and

- *leaves* though the outer curve $y=x.$

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(x)-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[x+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.
Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[x+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{4}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({[x+1]}^{2}-{[{x}^{4}+1]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y^2},$ and

- *leaves* though the outer curve $x=2y.$

$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y^2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/cca4c498956a16cb374a8d0b3341a09e52844026593557710525d07be79a233a.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,({y}^{2})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[2y+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({[2y+2]}^{2}-{[{y}^{2}+2]}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(-{y}^{4}+8y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}+4{y}^{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi [(-\frac{32}{5}+16)-0] \\  & =\frac{48\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
